Perpetually
per-pet'-ū-al-lī
adv. (continually, without interruption; in Scripture, of God's regard and of man's unrelenting anger)
Latin perpetuus, continuous, uninterrupted, from per and petere, to go through. The Authorized Version uses the adverb three times, twice of the eyes and heart of God upon His house, and once of a brother's wrath that would not stop.

Biblical Definition

Twice God says of the temple: “mine eyes and mine heart shall be there perpetually” (1Ki 9:3; 2Ch 7:16). The words are worth weighing separately. Eyes — His constant regard, the attention that never lapses. Heart — His affection, so that the place is not merely watched but loved. And perpetually — without interruption, not in seasons of favour alternating with seasons of absence. That is the promise on which every prayer toward the house in Solomon's dedication rests, and the New Testament transfers it without loss: the temple is now a people, builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit, and the eyes and heart are there perpetually still. The third use is the exact inversion, and it is chilling: of Edom, “he did pursue his brother with the sword, and did cast off all pity, and his anger did tear perpetually, and he kept his wrath for ever” (Amo 1:11). The same adverb, the same unbroken continuity — but of a hatred. Esau's descendants nursed a grievance against Jacob's for a thousand years and God finally judged it. The word therefore measures two permanences: God's settled love toward His dwelling place, and man's settled refusal to forgive his brother. Both are described as never letting go.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines perpetually as constantly, continually, incessantly; applied to that which has no intermission.

expand to see more

PERPETUALLY, adv. Constantly; continually; applied to things which proceed without intermission.

PERPETUAL, a. Never ceasing; continuing forever in future time; destined to be eternal.

1. Continuing or continued without intermission; uninterrupted; as a perpetual stream.

2. Everlasting; enduring; as a perpetual covenant; a perpetual statute.

Key Scripture

1Ki 9:3 — "And the LORD said unto him, I have heard thy prayer and thy supplication, that thou hast made before me: I have hallowed this house, which thou hast built, to put my name there for ever; and mine eyes and mine heart shall be there perpetually."

2Ch 7:16 — "For now have I chosen and sanctified this house, that my name may be there for ever: and mine eyes and mine heart shall be there perpetually."

Amo 1:11 — "Thus saith the LORD; For three transgressions of Edom, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because he did pursue his brother with the sword, and did cast off all pity, and his anger did tear perpetually, and he kept his wrath for ever:"

Modern Corruption

A grudge is now called boundaries or accountability; Amos calls perpetual anger against a brother a judged transgression.

expand to see more

Edom's sin in Amos 1:11 is not that he was wronged — Jacob genuinely wronged Esau — but that he kept the wrath, tearing perpetually, casting off all pity. Our own vocabulary has grown generous toward exactly this: the permanent estrangement is renamed as a boundary, the refusal to forgive as accountability, the cultivated grievance as processing. Some separations are lawful and even required, and Scripture provides for them. But it never provides for the perpetual anger itself. The unforgiving servant of Matthew 18 was delivered to the tormentors, and the sentence is attached to a warning that our Lord did not soften.

Set against it is the mercy of the other two verses. God's eyes and heart are perpetually upon His house — and He said it to Solomon, whose house would in time be defiled, whose kingdom would be torn, and whose temple would be burned. The perpetuity was not conditioned on the building's standing. That is the ground on which a man forgives his brother: he has been regarded perpetually by One who had every right to look away.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kol-hayyamim, all the days; netsach (H5331), perpetuity, unending duration; 'ad (H5703), for ever.

expand to see more

Hebrew kol-hayyamim — all the days, continually; 1 Kings 9:3 and 2 Chronicles 7:16, of God's eyes and heart upon the house.

Hebrew netsach (H5331) — perpetuity, enduring; Amos 1:11, his anger did tear perpetually.

Hebrew 'ebrah (H5678) — overflowing rage, wrath; the wrath Edom kept for ever.

Hebrew rachamim (H7356) — compassions, tender mercies; what Edom cast off.

Greek diapantos (G1275) — continually, through all; Luke 24:53, Hebrews 13:15, of praise offered continually.

Usage

"“Mine eyes and mine heart shall be there perpetually” — regard and affection, unbroken."

"“His anger did tear perpetually” — the same word, of a grudge."

"“He kept his wrath for ever” — and God kept an account of it."
